title: Gandhi meets the Gita
hookLine: a young law student is embarrassed to admit he hasn't read the Gita
carry: dwelling on a want slides into anger

cards: London, and a young Indian law student far from home.

Two brothers he's met, Theosophists interested in Indian thought, are reading the Bhagavad Gita in an English translation, Edwin Arnold's verse version, and they invite him to read the original with them.
And the young man has to admit something awkward. He has never read it. Not in Sanskrit, not in his own Gujarati.
He tells this story about himself later, in his autobiography, and he says he felt ashamed. The young man was Mohandas Gandhi.

teach.h: A BORROWED BOOK, READ WITH FRIENDS.
teach.b: So Gandhi's Gita begins in an unlikely place: friends from another country, an English verse translation, and a Sanskrit text he could only half follow.
He reads it with them, and some verses near the end of the second chapter strike him hard. They hold one of the Gita's best-known teachings: how a want takes over a mind, step by step.
A person dwells on the things the senses want.
From dwelling comes attachment. From attachment, desire. From desire, anger.
From anger, confusion. Memory slips, judgment fails, and the person is lost. Gandhi doesn't say he understood all of it then.
But the book stayed with him, and he came to prize it above other books for knowing truth. Later, in South Africa, he did something very ordinary with it.

teach.h: VERSES ON SLIPS BY THE WASHBASIN.
teach.b: He wrote verses on slips of paper, stuck them on the wall where he washed in the morning, and learned them by heart while getting ready for the day. Not in a temple. Next to the washbasin.

teach.h: DWELLING ON A WANT SLIDES INTO ANGER.
teach.b: The same chapter describes the one the Gita calls sthitaprajna, whose wisdom stands steady, who sees the slide starting and isn't carried off by every want and every fear.

Those verses became part of the daily prayers in the community he founded. Gandhi didn't arrive with the Gita already in hand. He came to it a little late, a little embarrassed, and then he kept it close.

how: In Gandhian ashrams the closing verses of the Gita's second chapter, on the one of steady wisdom, are recited as part of daily prayer, and some Hindus learn Gita verses by heart, a few at a time.

games.q: for an hour you've been staring at photos of the concert you couldn't get tickets for. your dad asks a simple question and you snap at him. what does the Gita's second chapter say just happened?
o: dwelling became attachment, attachment became desire, desire became anger.
games.why: Gita 2.62–63: dwelling on what the senses want breeds attachment, then desire, then anger, then confusion. these were the verses that struck Gandhi hard.

practice: Bring to mind one small want tugging at you today, a snack, a scroll, a reply you'd like to send, and watch the slide the Gita describes, slowly: the dwelling, the pull of it, the wanting, without scolding yourself.
Then let the attention rest on the breath, steady, the way the steady one in the Gita stays still while the wants come and go. If you pray, you can hold that steadiness in prayer.
